column1: # Hadith 1 — Actions are by intentions (Ibn Rajab's commentary, batch 1)

column2: ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

“Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended. So whoever’s emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever’s emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated.”
Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

Only Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī narrated this hadith, from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqāṣ al-Laythī, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), and it has no authentic route besides this one. So said ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and others.

Al-Khaṭṭābī said: I know of no disagreement among the hadith scholars about that. It has, however, been narrated from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd and others, and it has been said that it was narrated through many routes, but none of them is authentic in the view of the hadith masters (ḥuffāẓ).

Then a great many people, a vast multitude, narrated it from al-Anṣārī. It has been said that more than two hundred narrators reported it from him, and also that seven hundred did. Among the most eminent of them are Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, Ibn al-Mubārak, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Ḥammād ibn Zayd, Shuʿbah, Ibn ʿUyaynah and others.

The scholars agree that it is authentic and have received it with acceptance. Al-Bukhārī opened his book al-Ṣaḥīḥ with it, giving it the place of a preface, to indicate that every deed not done seeking the Face of Allah is void,

bearing no fruit in this world or the Hereafter. That is why ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī said: Were I to compile a book arranged in chapters, I would put the hadith of ʿUmar on actions being by intention in every chapter. He is also reported to have said: Whoever wants to compile a book should begin with the hadith “Actions are by intentions.”
This hadith is one of the hadiths around which the religion revolves. Al-Shāfiʿī is reported to have said: This hadith is a third of knowledge, and it enters into seventy chapters of jurisprudence.

Imam Aḥmad is reported to have said: The foundations of Islam rest on three hadiths: the hadith of ʿUmar, “Actions are by intentions”; the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, “Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that is not part of it, it is rejected”; and the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear.”

Al-Ḥākim said: We were told, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Aḥmad, from his father, that he mentioned the Prophet’s words (blessings and peace be upon him), “Actions are by intentions,” and his words, “The creation of each of you is gathered in his mother’s womb for forty days,”

and his words, “Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that is not part of it, it is rejected,” and said: Every compilation ought to begin with these hadiths, for they are the foundations of hadith.

Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh is reported to have said: Four hadiths are among the foundations of the religion: the hadith of ʿUmar, “Actions are only by intentions”; the hadith “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear”;
the hadith “The creation of each of you is gathered in his mother’s womb”; and the hadith “Whoever does anything in this matter of ours that is not part of it, it is rejected.”
ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd reported that Abū ʿUbayd said: The Prophet ﷺ gathered the whole affair of the Hereafter in one saying,

“Whoever introduces into our matter what is not part of it, it is rejected,” and he gathered the whole affair of this world in one saying, “Actions are only by intentions.” These two enter into every chapter.

Abū Dāwūd is reported to have said: I looked into the hadiths with connected chains (al-musnad) and found them to be four thousand hadiths. Then I looked again and found that those four thousand hadiths revolve around four: the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear”;

the hadith of ʿUmar, “Actions are only by intentions”; the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, “Allah is good and accepts only what is good, and Allah has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers…” to the end of the hadith; and the hadith “Part of the excellence of a person’s Islam is his leaving what does not concern him.”
He said: Each of these hadiths is a quarter of knowledge.
Abū Dāwūd is also reported to have said: I wrote down five hundred thousand hadiths from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ,

and from them I selected what I put into this book — meaning the Sunan. I gathered four thousand eight hundred hadiths in it, and four of them are enough for a person in his religion. The first is his saying ﷺ,
“Actions are only by intentions”; the second, his saying ﷺ, “Part of the excellence of a person’s Islam is his leaving what does not concern him”; the third, his saying ﷺ,
“The believer is not a believer until he is content for his brother with only what he is content with for himself”; and the fourth, his saying ﷺ, “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear.”
In another report he said: Jurisprudence revolves around five hadiths: “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear”; his saying ﷺ,

“There is to be no harm and no returning of harm”; his saying, “Actions are only by intentions”; his saying, “The religion is sincere counsel”; and his saying, “What I have forbidden you, avoid; and what I have commanded you, do as much of it as you are able.”

In another report he said: The foundations of the Sunnah in every field are four hadiths: the hadith of ʿUmar, “Actions are only by intentions”; the hadith “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear”;

the hadith “Part of the excellence of a person’s Islam is his leaving what does not concern him”; and the hadith “Be detached from this world and Allah will love you; be detached from what is in people’s hands and people will love you.”
The ḥāfiẓ Abū al-Ḥasan Ṭāhir ibn Mufawwiz al-Maʿāfirī al-Andalusī has these lines:
The mainstay of the religion, for us, is four sayings / from the words of the best of all creation:
“Beware of doubtful things, be detached, leave what / does not concern you, and act with intention.”
As for his saying ﷺ, “Actions are only by intentions” — and in another narration, “Actions are by intention” —
both wordings convey restriction, on the correct view; our purpose here is neither to account for that nor to discuss it at length.

Scholars have differed over what is to be understood as implied in his words “Actions are by intentions.” Many of the later scholars claim that the implied sense is: actions are valid, or count, or are accepted, by intentions. On this view, the actions meant are only those acts of the Sharīʿah that require an intention;

whatever does not require an intention — habits such as eating, drinking and dressing, or returning trusts and things one is liable for, such as deposits and goods taken by usurpation — needs no intention at all, and all of it is excluded from the general scope of the “actions” mentioned here.
Others said: On the contrary, “actions” here is fully general, and nothing is excluded from it.

Some have attributed this view to the majority, apparently meaning the majority of the early scholars. It occurs in the words of Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī, Abū Ṭālib al-Makkī and other early scholars, and it is the apparent sense of Imam Aḥmad’s words.
He said, in the report of Ḥanbal: I would like everyone who does a deed — prayer, fasting, charity,
or any kind of righteousness — to have the intention come first, before the act. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Actions are by intentions,” and this applies to every matter.
Al-Faḍl ibn Ziyād said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh — meaning Aḥmad — about intention in action. I said: What is intention?
He said: A person works on himself so that, when he wants to do a deed, he does not intend people by it.
Aḥmad ibn Dāwūd al-Ḥarbī said: Yazīd ibn Hārūn narrated the hadith of ʿUmar, “Actions are only by intentions,” while Aḥmad was sitting there, and Aḥmad said to Yazīd: Abū Khālid, this is the noose.

On this view, some said that the implied sense is: actions occur, or come about, through intentions. It is then a statement about voluntary actions: that they only happen from an intent on the part of the doer, which is what causes them to be done and to exist. His words that follow,

“and every person shall have only what he intended,” are then a statement of the Sharīʿah’s ruling: that the doer’s share of his deed is his intention. If the intention is righteous, the deed is righteous and he has its reward; if it is corrupt, the deed is corrupt and he bears its sin.

It is also possible that what is implied in his words “Actions are by intentions” is: actions are righteous or corrupt, accepted or rejected, rewarded or unrewarded, according to intentions. It is then a statement of a ruling of the Sharīʿah,

namely that whether deeds are righteous or corrupt follows whether intentions are righteous or corrupt — like his saying ﷺ, “Actions are only by their endings,” meaning that whether they are righteous or corrupt, accepted or not, depends on how they end.
His words after that, “and every person shall have only what he intended,” tell us that a person gains from his deed only what he intended by it: if he intended good, he gains good,

and if he intended evil by it, he gains evil. This is not a mere repetition of the first sentence. The first sentence shows that whether a deed is righteous or corrupt depends on the intention that brings it into being,

while the second shows that the doer’s reward for his deed depends on his righteous intention, and his punishment for it on his corrupt intention. His intention may also be merely permissible, in which case the deed is permissible and brings him neither reward nor punishment.

So whether the deed in itself is righteous, corrupt or permissible depends on the intention that prompts it and brings it into existence; and whether the doer is rewarded, punished or simply left unharmed depends on the intention through which the deed became righteous, corrupt or permissible.
Know that intention (niyyah), in the language, is a kind of aim (qaṣd) and will (irādah), although distinctions have been drawn between these words that this is not the place to mention.
In the usage of the scholars, intention has two meanings.

The first is distinguishing acts of worship from one another — distinguishing the noon (ẓuhr) prayer from the afternoon (ʿaṣr) prayer, for example, or the fast of Ramaḍān from other fasts — or distinguishing acts of worship from ordinary habits,
such as distinguishing the ritual bath for major impurity from a bath taken to cool off or to get clean, and the like. This is the intention so often found in the jurists’ discussions in their books.
The second meaning is distinguishing what the deed is aimed at: whether it is for Allah alone, without partner, or for someone else, or for Allah and someone else together.

This is the intention that those who know Allah (al-ʿārifūn) discuss in their books when they speak about sincerity and what goes with it, and it is what is so often found in the words of the early Salaf.

Abū Bakr ibn Abī al-Dunyā compiled a work he named Kitāb al-Ikhlāṣ wa-l-Niyyah (“Sincerity and Intention”), and it was this intention he meant. It is the intention that is mentioned again and again in the words of the Prophet ﷺ, sometimes with the word “intention”,

sometimes with the word “will”, and sometimes with a word close to these; and it is mentioned often in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with words other than “intention” too, words close to it in meaning.
Those who distinguished between intention on the one hand and will, aim and the like on the other did so

only because they supposed that intention is confined to the first meaning, the one the jurists mention. Some of them said: Intention is confined to the intender’s own act, whereas will is not; a person may will that Allah forgive him, but he does not “intend” it.
We have mentioned that intention, in the words of the Prophet ﷺ and the Salaf of this nation, mostly refers to this second meaning; in that case it means will.

That is why the Qurʾān so often expresses it with words of willing and desiring (irādah), as in His words, Exalted is He: “Among you are some who desire this world, and among you are some who desire the Hereafter” [Āl ʿImrān 3:152]; His words: “You desire the goods of this world, while Allah desires the Hereafter” [al-Anfāl 8:67]; His words:

“Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase him in his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We give him some of it, but in the Hereafter he has no share” [al-Shūrā 42:20]; His words:

“Whoever desires the fleeting life, We hasten for him in it whatever We will, for whomever We wish; then We appoint for him Hell, which he will enter, condemned and rejected. And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as it deserves, while he is a believer — the striving of those will be appreciated” [al-Isrāʾ 17:18–19];

His words, Exalted is He: “Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We repay them in full for their deeds in it, and they are not deprived in it. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire; what they did in it has come to nothing, and vain is what they used to do” [Hūd 11:15–16];
His words: “Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face” [al-Anʿām 6:52]; His words:

“Keep yourself patiently with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His Face, and do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the life of this world” [al-Kahf 18:28]; and His words:

“That is best for those who desire the Face of Allah, and it is they who will prosper. Whatever you give in usury to grow within people’s wealth does not grow with Allah; but whatever you give in zakāh, desiring the Face of Allah — it is they who will have it multiplied” [al-Rūm 30:38–39].

Sometimes the Qurʾān expresses it with the word “seeking” (ibtighāʾ), as in His words, Exalted is He: “only seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High” [al-Layl 92:20]; His words: “The example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:265]; His words: “You do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:272];

and His words: “There is no good in much of their private talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or setting things right between people; and whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We shall give him a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:114].
So He denied that there is any good in much of what people talk about privately, except enjoining what is right; and among its instances He singled out charity and setting things right between people

because of how widely they benefit. This shows that conferring privately about such things is good. As for being rewarded for it by Allah, He reserved that for whoever does it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

He made enjoining what is right — charity, setting things right between people and the like — good even when it is not done seeking the Face of Allah, because of the benefit it brings to others: people receive kindness and good through it. As for the one who does the enjoining,
if he intends by it the Face of Allah and seeks His pleasure, it is good for him and he is rewarded for it; if he does not intend that, it is not good for him,
and he has no reward for it. This is unlike someone who fasts, prays and remembers Allah with the aim of gaining the goods of this world: there is no good for him in it at all,
since it brings no benefit to the one who does it, because of the sin it entails, nor to anyone else,
since its benefit passes on to no one — unless, perhaps, someone follows his example in it.

As for the Sunnah and the words of the Salaf calling this meaning “intention”, there is a great deal, and we will mention some of it. Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit,
that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever goes out on campaign in the path of Allah intending nothing but a camel’s hobbling cord shall have what he intended.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Most of the martyrs of my nation are those who die in their beds, and many a man killed between the two battle lines — Allah knows best what his intention was.”

Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Jābir, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “People will be gathered according to their intentions”; and from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “People will only be raised according to their intentions.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded, from the hadith of ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Those who fight one another will only be raised according to their intentions.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Umm Salamah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Someone will seek refuge in the House, and an army will be sent against him; when they are in an open stretch of desert, the earth will swallow them.” I said: O Messenger of Allah, what of someone who was there unwillingly?
He said: “He will be swallowed up with them, but he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection according to his intention.”

Also in it, from ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet ﷺ is reported with the same meaning, and in it he said: “They will perish in a single destruction but come forth to different destinations; Allah will raise them according to their intentions.”
Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thābit, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever has this world as his concern, Allah will scatter his affairs,

put his poverty before his eyes, and nothing of this world will come to him except what was written for him. Whoever has the Hereafter as his intention, Allah will gather his affairs for him, put his richness in his heart, and this world will come to him in spite of itself.”

This is the wording of Ibn Mājah. Aḥmad’s wording is: “whoever has the Hereafter as his concern” and “whoever has this world as his intention.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it too, and his version has: “whoever has this world as his intention” and “whoever has the Hereafter as his intention.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, the Prophet ﷺ said: “You will never spend anything seeking by it the Face of Allah without being rewarded for it — even the morsel you put in your wife’s mouth.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā reported, with a broken chain, that ʿUmar said: There is no deed for one who has no intention, and no reward for one who does not seek reward — that is, no reward for one who does not look to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the reward of his deed.

And, with a weak chain, that Ibn Masʿūd said: Speech is of no benefit without action; speech and action are of no benefit without intention; and speech, action and intention are of no benefit unless they accord with the Sunnah.
Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: Learn intention, for it reaches further than action.

Zubayd al-Yāmī said: I love to have an intention in everything, even in eating and drinking. He is also reported to have said: In everything you set out to do, intend good — even in going out to the rubbish heap.
Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī said: I have seen that all good is gathered together by good intention, and that is good enough for you even if you do not toil.
Dāwūd said: Righteousness is the aspiration of the God-fearing. Even if all his limbs were attached to love of this world, his intention would one day bring him back to his origin.
Sufyān al-Thawrī said: I have never dealt with anything harder for me than my intention,
because it keeps turning on me.
Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ said: Purifying the intention of what corrupts it is harder on those who act than long striving.
Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr was asked: Will you not attend the funeral?
He said: Wait until I make an intention. The narrator said: He reflected for a moment, then said: Go on.
Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbdillāh said: The heart is set right by setting action right, and action is set right by setting intention right.

One of the Salaf said: Whoever would be glad to have his deed made complete, let him make his intention good, for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, rewards the servant when his intention is good — even for a morsel of food.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: Many a small deed is made great by its intention, and many a great deed is made small by its intention.
Ibn ʿAjlān said: Action is sound only with three things: taqwā of Allah, good intention, and getting it right.
Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: What Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, wants from you is only your intention and your will.
Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ said: Preferring Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is better than being killed in His path.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded all of this in Kitāb al-Ikhlāṣ wa-l-Niyyah.

In it he also reported, with a broken chain, that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The best of deeds are carrying out what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made obligatory, scrupulously avoiding what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made unlawful, and truthfulness of intention towards what is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

This makes clear the meaning of what is reported from Imam Aḥmad, that the foundations of Islam are three hadiths: the hadith “Actions are by intentions”, the hadith “Whoever introduces into our matter what is not part of it, it is rejected”, and the hadith “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear.”
For the whole religion comes down to doing what is commanded, leaving what is forbidden and holding back from doubtful matters, and all of this is contained in the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr.
This is only complete with two things.
The first is that the deed, outwardly, conforms to the Sunnah. This is what the hadith of ʿĀʾishah contains: “Whoever introduces into our matter what is not part of it, it is rejected.”
The second is that the deed, inwardly, is aimed at the Face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as the hadith of ʿUmar contains: “Actions are by intentions.”
Al-Fuḍayl said, about His words, Exalted is He, “that He may test you, which of you is best in deed” [al-Mulk 67:2]: The most sincere of it and the most correct.

He said: If a deed is sincere but not correct, it is not accepted; and if it is correct but not sincere, it is not accepted — not until it is both sincere and correct. He said: Sincere is when it is for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and correct is when it accords with the Sunnah.

What al-Fuḍayl said is shown by the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord” [al-Kahf 18:110].
One of those who know Allah said: They surpassed one another only through their intentions; they did not surpass one another through fasting and prayer.

His words ﷺ: “So whoever’s emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever’s emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated.”
Having said that actions follow intentions, and that the doer’s share of his deed is his intention, whether good or evil — two comprehensive statements and universal principles

from which nothing falls outside — he ﷺ then gave an example of deeds that are identical in form but whose soundness and corruption differ as intentions differ, as though he were saying: all other deeds follow the pattern of this example.

The root meaning of emigration (hijrah) is leaving the land of shirk and moving from it to the abode of Islam, as the Emigrants before the conquest of Makkah used to emigrate from it to the city of the Prophet ﷺ; and some of them had earlier emigrated to the land of Abyssinia, to the Negus.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that this emigration differs with the intentions and aims behind it. Whoever emigrates to the abode of Islam out of love for Allah and His Messenger, desiring to learn the religion of Islam

and to practise his religion openly where he had been unable to do so in the abode of shirk, is the true emigrant to Allah and His Messenger; and it is honour and pride enough for him that he attains what he intended by his emigration to Allah and His Messenger.
It is for this reason that the answer to this condition simply repeats its wording,
because attaining what he intended by his emigration is the ultimate goal in this world and the Hereafter.

Whoever’s emigration from the land of shirk to the abode of Islam was in pursuit of some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry in the abode of Islam, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated. The first is a merchant and the second a suitor, and neither of them is an emigrant.
His words “to that for which he emigrated” belittle and disdain the worldly thing he sought, since he did not even name it.
Moreover, emigration to Allah and His Messenger is a single thing that admits no plurality, and so he repeated the answer with the wording of the condition.

Emigration for worldly ends, on the other hand, has no limit: a person may emigrate in pursuit of something worldly that is at one time permissible and at another unlawful, and the worldly things sought by emigration are countless. That is why he said, “his emigration is to that for which he emigrated” — that is, whatever it may be.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), concerning His words, Exalted is He, “When believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them” [al-Mumtaḥanah 60:10], to the end of the verse,

that he said: When a woman came to the Prophet ﷺ, he would have her swear by Allah that she had not left out of hatred for a husband; by Allah that she had not left out of a preference for one land over another; by Allah that she had not left in search of something worldly; and by Allah that she had left only out of love for Allah and His Messenger.
Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Jarīr, and al-Bazzār in his Musnad recorded it, and al-Tirmidhī recorded it in abridged form in some copies of his book.
Wakīʿ reported in his book, from al-Aʿmash, from Shaqīq — that is, Abū Wāʾil — who said: A Bedouin from our clan proposed to a woman called Umm Qays.
She refused to marry him until he emigrated, so he emigrated and she married him, and we used to call him the Emigrant of Umm Qays.
He said: ʿAbdullāh — meaning Ibn Masʿūd — said: Whoever emigrates seeking something, it is his.
This wording implies that this did not happen in the time of the Prophet ﷺ but in the time of Ibn Masʿūd. It has, however, been narrated by way of Sufyān al-Thawrī, from al-Aʿmash,

from Abū Wāʾil, from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: There was a man among us who proposed to a woman called Umm Qays. She refused to marry him until he emigrated, so he emigrated and married her, and we used to call him the Emigrant of Umm Qays.
Ibn Masʿūd said: Whoever emigrates for something, it is his.
It has become well known that the story of the Emigrant of Umm Qays was the occasion for the Prophet’s words ﷺ,

“whoever’s emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry.” Many later scholars mention this in their books, but we have not seen any basis for it with an authentic chain. Allah knows best.
All other deeds are like emigration in this respect: whether they are sound or corrupt depends on the intention that prompts them — jihād, Ḥajj and the rest.
The Prophet ﷺ was asked about people’s differing intentions in jihād and what they aim at by it — showing off, displaying courage, partisanship and so on — and which of these is in the path of Allah.
He said: “Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is uppermost, he is in the path of Allah.” This excluded every worldly aim they had asked about.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī: A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, one man fights for the spoils, another fights to be talked about, and another fights so that his standing may be seen — which of them is in the path of Allah?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is uppermost, he is in the path of Allah.”

In a version in Muslim: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about a man who fights out of courage, fights out of tribal zeal, and fights to show off — which of these is in the path of Allah? And he mentioned the hadith.
In another of his versions: A man fights out of anger, and fights out of tribal zeal.
Al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: What do you think of a man who goes on campaign seeking reward and renown — what does he get?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “He gets nothing.” Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Allah accepts no deed except one that is sincere and by which His Face is sought.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that a man said: O Messenger of Allah, what of a man who wants to go on jihād while seeking some of the goods of this world?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “He has no reward.” The man put it to him three times, and each time the Prophet ﷺ said: “He has no reward.”
Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are two kinds of campaign. As for one who seeks the Face of Allah, obeys the leader,

spends the best of his wealth, is easy on his comrade and avoids corruption, his sleeping and his waking are all reward. As for one who campaigns out of pride, to be seen and to be heard of, disobeys the leader and spreads corruption in the land, he does not even come back breaking even.”

Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me about jihād and campaigning. He said: “If you fight with patience, seeking the reward from Allah,

Allah will raise you patient and seeking the reward; and if you fight to show off and to vie in plenty, Allah will raise you showing off and vying in plenty. In whatever state you fight or are killed, in that state Allah will raise you.”

Muslim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought, and He will make known to him His blessings upon him, and he will acknowledge them. He will say: What did you do with them?
He will say: I fought for You until I was martyred. He will say: You have lied. Rather, you fought

so that it would be said, ‘He is brave,’ and so it was said. Then the command will be given, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire. And a man who learned knowledge and taught it, and recited the Qurʾān. He will be brought, and He will make known to him His blessings upon him, and he will acknowledge them. He will say: What did you do with them?
He will say: I learned knowledge and taught it, and recited the Qurʾān for Your sake.

He will say: You have lied. Rather, you learned knowledge so that it would be said, ‘He is a scholar,’ and you recited the Qurʾān so that it would be said, ‘He is a reciter,’ and so it was said. Then the command will be given, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire.

And a man to whom Allah gave abundance and granted every kind of wealth. He will be brought, and He will make known to him His blessings upon him, and he will acknowledge them. He will say: What did you do with them?

He will say: I left no path in which You love wealth to be spent without spending in it for Your sake. He will say: You have lied. Rather, you did it so that it would be said, ‘He is generous,’ and so it was said. Then the command will be given, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire.”

The hadith also relates that when this hadith reached Muʿāwiyah, he wept until he fainted. When he came round, he said: Allah and His Messenger have spoken the truth. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We repay them in full for their deeds in it, and they are not deprived in it. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire” [Hūd 11:15–16].

A threat has also come concerning those who learn knowledge for other than the Face of Allah, as Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah recorded from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him),

that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever learns knowledge of the kind by which the Face of Allah is sought, learning it only to gain some of the goods of this world, will not find the ʿarf of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection” — meaning its fragrance.

Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Kaʿb ibn Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever seeks knowledge to argue with the foolish, or to vie with the scholars, or to turn people’s faces towards himself, Allah will admit him into the Fire.”
Ibn Mājah recorded it with the same meaning from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, Ḥudhayfah and Jābir, from the Prophet ﷺ. The wording of Jābir’s hadith is:
“Do not learn knowledge to vaunt yourselves before the scholars, nor to argue with the foolish, nor to claim the best seats in gatherings with it. Whoever does that — the Fire, the Fire!”

Ibn Masʿūd said: Do not learn knowledge for three things: to argue with the foolish, to dispute with the jurists, or to turn people’s faces towards yourselves. Seek with your words and deeds what is with Allah, for that remains and everything else passes away.
A threat has also come concerning acting for other than Allah in general, as Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ,

who said: “Give this nation glad tidings of eminence, high standing, religion and establishment in the land. Whoever among them does a deed of the Hereafter for the sake of this world will have no share in the Hereafter.”
Know that action for other than Allah takes several forms. Sometimes it is pure showing off, in which nothing is intended except to be seen by created beings for some worldly purpose,

like the state of the hypocrites in their prayer, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to people, and they remember Allah only a little” [al-Nisāʾ 4:142].
The Exalted also says: “So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, those who show off” [al-Māʿūn 107:4–6], to the end of the passage.

Allah the Exalted likewise described the disbelievers as showing off, in His words: “Do not be like those who came out of their homes boastfully and to be seen by people, and who turn others from the path of Allah” [al-Anfāl 8:47].
This pure showing off hardly ever comes from a believer in the obligatory prayer and fasting, though it may occur in obligatory charity, in the Ḥajj and in other outward deeds,
or deeds whose benefit extends to others, for sincerity in these is rare. No Muslim doubts that such a deed has come to nothing and that the one who does it deserves Allah’s loathing and punishment.
At other times the deed is for Allah but showing off has a share in it. If it shares in it from the outset, the authentic texts show that it too is invalid and has come to nothing.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, says:

I am the partner most free of need of any partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his partner.” Ibn Mājah recorded it, and his wording is: “I am quit of him, and it belongs to the one he associated.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from Shaddād ibn Aws, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever prays to be seen has committed shirk; whoever fasts to be seen has committed shirk;

and whoever gives charity to be seen has committed shirk. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: I am the best of sharers for whoever associates anything with Me: the whole of his deed, little and much, goes to the partner he associated with Me, and I have no need of it.”
Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd ibn Abī Faḍālah — who was one of the Companions — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“When Allah gathers the first and the last for a Day about which there is no doubt, a caller will call out: Whoever associated anyone in a deed he did for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, let him seek its reward from someone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for Allah is the partner most free of need of any partnership.”

Al-Bazzār recorded in his Musnad, from the hadith of al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: I am the best of partners; whoever associates a partner with Me, it belongs to My partner.
O people, make your deeds sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic,

for Allah accepts only those deeds done sincerely for Him. Do not say: This is for Allah and for kinship, for then it is for kinship and none of it is for Allah. And do not say: This is for Allah and for your sakes, for then it is for your sakes and none of it is for Allah.”

Al-Nasāʾī recorded with a sound chain, from Abū Umāmah al-Bāhilī, that a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, what do you think of a man who goes on campaign seeking reward and renown?
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “He gets nothing.” He repeated it three times, and each time the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him:
“He gets nothing.” Then he said: “Allah accepts no deed except one done sincerely for Him and by which His Face is sought.”
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: A man said: O Messenger of Allah, I take my stand [in battle] seeking the Face of Allah, and I want my position to be seen.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave him no reply until this was revealed: “So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord” [al-Kahf 18:110].

Among those from whom this meaning has been reported — that a deed mixed with any showing off is void — is a group of the Salaf, among them ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, Abū al-Dardāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and others.
Among the mursal reports of al-Qāsim ibn Mukhaymirah is that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah does not accept a deed in which there is a mustard seed’s weight of showing off.”
We know of no disagreement about this among the Salaf, though there is disagreement over it on the part of some later scholars.

If the intention of jihād, for example, is mixed with an intention other than showing off — such as taking a wage for service, taking some of the spoils, or trading — the reward of their jihād is reduced by it, but not voided altogether.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “When those who go on campaign take spoils, they have received two-thirds of their reward in advance; if they take no spoils, their reward is complete.”
We have mentioned above hadiths showing that whoever intends some worldly goods by his jihād has no reward. These are taken to refer to someone who had no aim in jihād but this world.

Imam Aḥmad said: The merchant, the hired man and the one who hires out his animals are rewarded in proportion to how much of their intention in their campaign is sincere, and none of them is like one who strives with his person and his wealth and mixes nothing else with it.

He also said, about someone who takes a payment for jihād: If he did not go out for the sake of the dirhams, there is no harm in his taking it — it is as though he went out for his religion, and when he is given something he takes it.

Something similar is reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: If one of you has resolved on going on campaign and Allah compensates him with some provision, there is no harm in that. But as for one of you who goes on campaign if he is given a dirham and stays behind if he is denied a dirham, there is no good in that.
Al-Awzāʿī said likewise: If the campaigner’s intention is set on the campaign, I see no harm in it.

The same is said of someone who takes something in the Ḥajj in order to perform the Ḥajj with it, whether for himself or on behalf of someone else. Mujāhid is reported to have said, about the Ḥajj of the camel-hirer, the hired man and the merchant:
It is complete; nothing is taken from their reward. This is taken to mean that their original aim was the Ḥajj and not earning.

If the deed was originally for Allah and then an intention of showing off came upon it, and it was a passing thought that he pushed away, it does him no harm, without disagreement. But if he went along with it, is his deed voided, or does it not harm him, so that he is recompensed according to his original intention?

The scholars of the Salaf disagree over this, as Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī related, and both preferred the view that his deed is not voided by it and that he is recompensed according to his first intention. This is reported from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others.
This view is supported by what Abū Dāwūd recorded in his Marāsīl from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī: A man said: O Messenger of Allah,
the Banū Salimah all fight. Some of them fight for this world, some fight out of gallantry, and some fight seeking the Face of Allah. Which of them is the martyr?
He said: “All of them, if the root of his concern is that the word of Allah should be uppermost.”

Ibn Jarīr mentioned that this disagreement concerns only deeds whose end is bound to their beginning, such as prayer, fasting and the Ḥajj. Deeds without such a connection, such as recitation, remembrance, spending wealth and spreading knowledge, are cut off by an intention of showing off that comes upon them, and need a renewed intention.

Similarly, it is reported that Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī said: Sometimes I narrate a hadith with an intention, and when I am partway through it my intention changes; so a single hadith needs several intentions.

Jihād, as in the mursal report of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, is no objection to this, for jihād becomes binding once a person is present in the battle line and may not then be abandoned, so it becomes like the Ḥajj.

If, however, he does the deed sincerely for Allah, and then Allah puts good praise of him for it in the hearts of the believers, and he rejoices at Allah’s bounty and mercy and is glad of it, that does him no harm.
It is in this sense that the hadith of Abū Dharr came, from the Prophet ﷺ: he was asked about a man who does a good deed for Allah and people praise him for it,
and he said: “That is the believer’s glad tidings given in advance.” Muslim recorded it. Ibn Mājah also recorded it, and his version has: a man does a deed for Allah and people love him for it.
Imam Aḥmad, Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī and others explained it in this sense.

Likewise the hadith that al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah: A man said: O Messenger of Allah, a man does a deed and keeps it secret, and when it is discovered it pleases him. He said: “He has two rewards: the reward of secrecy and the reward of openness.”
Let us confine ourselves to this much discussion of sincerity and showing off, for it is sufficient.
In sum, how excellent are the words of Sahl ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Tustarī: Nothing is harder on the self than sincerity,
because it has no share in it.
Yūsuf ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Rāzī said: The rarest thing in this world is sincerity. How hard I strive to drive showing off out of my heart, yet it seems to sprout there again in another colour.
Ibn ʿUyaynah said: Among the supplications of Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbdillāh was: O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness for what I repented to You of and then went back to;

I seek Your forgiveness for what I bound myself to do for You and then did not fulfil for You; and I seek Your forgiveness for what I claimed I did seeking Your Face, when my heart was mixed with what You know.
Section

As for intention in the sense the jurists mention, which is distinguishing acts of worship from habits and distinguishing acts of worship from one another: abstaining from food and drink, for example, sometimes happens as a diet,

sometimes through inability to eat, and sometimes as giving up desires for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So fasting needs an intention to distinguish it from leaving food in any other way.
Likewise acts of worship such as prayer and fasting: some are obligatory and some voluntary.

The obligatory is of various kinds. The obligatory prayers are five every day and night; the obligatory fast is sometimes the fast of Ramaḍān, and sometimes the fast of an expiation or of a vow. None of this is distinguished except by intention.

Charity, likewise, may be voluntary or obligatory, and the obligatory may be zakāh or an expiation, and this too is distinguished only by intention. All of this falls under the general meaning of his words ﷺ: “and every person shall have only what he intended.”

There is a well-known disagreement among scholars over some of this. Some do not require the intention for an obligatory prayer to specify which prayer it is: in their view it is enough to intend the obligation of the time, even if he does not call its name to mind at that moment. This is one of the reported positions of Imam Aḥmad.
It follows from this view that whoever missed one prayer of a day and night and forgot which it was must make up three prayers: fajr, maghrib and one four-unit prayer.
A group of scholars likewise held that the fast of Ramaḍān does not need a specifying intention either, but is valid with an intention to fast in general,
because its time admits no other fast. This too is one of the reported positions of Imam Aḥmad.
It has sometimes been related of some of them that the fast of Ramaḍān needs no intention at all,
because it is specified by its very nature, so that it is like returning deposits; and al-Awzāʿī is related to have held the same about zakāh.
Some interpreted his view to mean that it is valid with an intention of charity in general, as with the Ḥajj.
Abū Ḥanīfah likewise said: If someone gave away the whole niṣāb in charity without any intention, it would count as his zakāh.
It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he heard a man pronouncing the talbiyah for Ḥajj on behalf of another man, and said to him: “Have you performed Ḥajj for yourself?”
He said: No. He said: “This one is for yourself; then perform Ḥajj for the man.”
The authenticity of this hadith has been questioned, but it is authentic from Ibn ʿAbbās and others.

Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad in the well-known position reported from him, and others took this to mean that the Ḥajj of Islam is discharged by an unspecified intention of Ḥajj, whether the person intended a voluntary Ḥajj or something else, and that specifying the intention is not a condition of Ḥajj. So if someone performs Ḥajj on behalf of another without having performed it for himself,

it counts for himself; likewise, if he performs Ḥajj for a vow, or as a voluntary act, without having performed the Ḥajj of Islam, it is converted into that. It is established that the Prophet ﷺ, in the Farewell Pilgrimage, after his Companions had entered [iḥrām] with him,

circumambulated [the Kaʿbah] and walked [between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah], commanded them to cancel their Ḥajj and make it an ʿUmrah. Some of them were combining Ḥajj with ʿUmrah and some performing Ḥajj alone, and their circumambulation on arrival was only the circumambulation of arrival, which is not obligatory; yet he commanded them to make it the circumambulation of ʿUmrah, which is obligatory.

Imam Aḥmad adopted this in the matter of cancelling Ḥajj and acted on it, yet it is problematic on his own principles, since he requires the obligatory circumambulation of Ḥajj and ʿUmrah to be specified by intention — on which most jurists, such as Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah, disagreed with him.

Imam Aḥmad may distinguish between a circumambulation performed in an iḥrām that has been converted — such as the iḥrām one cancels and makes into an ʿUmrah, where the circumambulation is converted along with the iḥrām, just as the circumambulation is converted in an iḥrām entered with a voluntary intention by someone who still owes the Ḥajj of Islam,

following the conversion of his iḥrām from its root and its counting towards his obligation — and the case of someone who performs the circumambulation of the visit (ṭawāf al-ziyārah) with the intention of the farewell circumambulation, or as a voluntary one. This does not count for him, because he did not intend the obligation by it, nor was it converted into an obligation following a conversion of his iḥrām. Allah knows best.
One case that falls under this topic: a man in the time of the Prophet ﷺ had left his charity with another man, and the son of the man giving the charity came and took it from the one who held it.

His father learned of this and brought the dispute to the Prophet ﷺ, saying [to his son]: It was not you I intended. The Prophet ﷺ said to the giver: “You have what you intended,” and to the one who took it: “You have what you took.” Al-Bukhārī recorded it.

Imam Aḥmad adopted this hadith and acted on it in what is explicitly reported from him, even though most of his followers hold otherwise. For a man is barred from giving his charity to his own child only for fear of favouritism;

when it reaches his child without his knowing, there is no favouritism, and the child is, in reality, among those entitled to charity. That is why, if he gave his charity to someone he thought poor who was in reality rich, it would count for him on the correct view,
since he gave only to someone he believed entitled, and poverty is a hidden matter whose reality can hardly be known.

As for ritual purification, the disagreement over whether intention is a condition for it is well known. It comes down to whether purification for prayer is an act of worship in its own right or one of the conditions of prayer, like removing filth and covering one’s nakedness.

Those who do not make intention a condition for it treat it like the other conditions of prayer; those who do make intention a condition treat it as an act of worship in its own right, and since it is an act of worship in itself, it is not valid without an intention. This is the view of the majority of scholars,

and its correctness is shown by the many authentic texts from the Prophet ﷺ that wuḍūʾ expiates sins and wrongdoings, and that whoever performs wuḍūʾ as he was commanded, it is an expiation for his sins.

This shows that the wuḍūʾ commanded in the Qurʾān is an act of worship in its own right, since the expiation of sins was made to follow from it; and wuḍūʾ devoid of intention expiates no sins, by agreement, so it is not what was commanded and prayer is not valid with it.
That is why none of the other conditions of prayer, such as removing filth and covering one’s nakedness, carries the reward that has come for wuḍūʾ.

If he combines the intention of wuḍūʾ with the aim of cooling off, or of removing filth or dirt, it suffices according to the explicit text of al-Shāfiʿī, and this is the view of most of Aḥmad’s followers,
because such an aim is neither unlawful nor disliked. That is why, if along with lifting ritual impurity he also intended to teach wuḍūʾ, it would not harm him.
The Prophet ﷺ would sometimes intend by his prayer to teach it to people, and likewise with the Ḥajj, as he said: “Take your rites from me.”
Among the areas of knowledge into which intention enters are questions of oaths.

An unintended oath requires no expiation: it is what runs on the tongue without the heart aiming at it, like saying “No, by Allah” and “Yes, by Allah” in the course of speech. The Exalted said: “Allah does not take you to task for what is unintended in your oaths, but He takes you to task for what your hearts have earned” [al-Baqarah 2:225].

Likewise, in oaths, one goes back to the intention of the one who swears and what he meant by his oath. If he swore by divorce or by the freeing of a slave, and then claimed he had intended something other than the apparent sense of his words, he is believed in what is between him and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Is it accepted from him in the outward judicial ruling?

There are two well-known views among scholars on this, and they are two reported positions of Aḥmad. It is reported of ʿUmar that a man was brought before him whose wife had said to him: Describe me with a likeness.

He said: You are like a gazelle, you are like a dove. She said: I will not be satisfied until you say: You are khaliyyah ṭāliq [“unfettered and let loose”, words also used for divorce]. So he said it, and ʿUmar said: Take her by the hand; she is your wife.
Abū ʿUbayd recorded it, and said: He meant the she-camel that is hobbled and then let loose from her hobble and left free: she is khaliyyah, free of the hobble, and she is ṭāliq,
because she has been let loose from it. The man meant that, so ʿUmar waived the divorce from him because of his intention.

He said: This is a basis for anyone who says something resembling the wording of divorce or manumission while intending something else: his own word is what counts in what is between him and Allah, and in the judicial ruling according to the interpretation of ʿUmar’s position (may Allah be pleased with him).

It is reported that Sumayṭ al-Sadūsī said: I proposed to a woman, and they said: We will not marry her to you until you divorce your wife. I said: I have divorced her three times. So they married her to me. Then they looked, and there was my wife still with me. They said: Did you not divorce her three times?

I said: I had So-and-so and divorced her, and So-and-so and divorced her, and So-and-so and divorced her; as for this one, I have not divorced her. I went to Shaqīq ibn Thawr, who was about to set out to ʿUthmān with a delegation, and said to him: Ask the Commander of the Believers about this. He went and asked him, and he said: His intention [decides it].
Abū ʿUbayd recorded it in Kitāb al-Ṭalāq, and related the consensus of the scholars on the like of this.
Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr said: I said to Aḥmad: Do you know the hadith of al-Sumayṭ?
He said: Yes — al-Sadūsī. He made the matter depend on his intention: Shaqīq mentioned it to ʿUthmān, and he made it depend on his intention.

If the one swearing is a wrongdoer, however, and intends something other than what his opponent made him swear to, his intention is of no benefit to him. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Your oath is according to what your companion takes you to be affirming.”
In another version of his: “The oath is according to the intention of the one who requires it.” This is taken to refer to the wrongdoer; as for the one wronged, his intention benefits him.
Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Suwayd ibn Ḥanẓalah, who said: We set out to go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr was with us. An enemy of his seized him,

and the people were reluctant to swear, so I swore that he was my brother, and he let him go. We came to the Prophet ﷺ and I told him that the people had been reluctant to swear and that I had sworn he was my brother. He said: “You spoke the truth: the Muslim is the brother of the Muslim.”
Intention likewise enters into divorce and manumission: if someone uses one of the indirect expressions that could mean divorce or manumission, an intention is required.
Can the evidence of the circumstances — anger, or a request for divorce and the like — take the place of intention or not?

There is a well-known disagreement among scholars about this. And in that case does the divorce take effect inwardly, as if he had intended it, or is it binding on him only in the outward judicial ruling?

There is a well-known disagreement about this too. If he pronounces divorce with an obvious indirect expression, such as al-battah [“irrevocably”] and the like, does it count as three divorces, or one?

There are two well-known views. The apparent position of Aḥmad’s school is that it counts as three when the intention is unspecified, while if he intended fewer than three by it, what he intended takes effect. Another position is also related from him: that three are binding on him in that case too.
If he saw a woman, thought she was his wife and divorced her, and she then turned out to be a stranger, his wife is divorced,
because it was only his wife he meant to divorce.

Aḥmad stated this explicitly; another position is related from him, that she is not divorced, which is the view of al-Shāfiʿī. If it were the other way round — he saw a woman he thought was a stranger, divorced her, and she turned out to be his wife — is she divorced?
There are two views, which are two reported positions of Aḥmad; the well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī’s school and of others is that she is divorced.

If he had two wives and forbade one of them to go out, then saw a woman who had gone out and, thinking she was the one he had forbidden, said to her: So-and-so, you went out — you are divorced, the scholars differ over the case. Al-Ḥasan said: The one forbidden is divorced,
because she is the one he intended.
Ibrāhīm said: Both are divorced. ʿAṭāʾ said: Neither of them is divorced. Aḥmad’s position is that the one forbidden is divorced, with no variation in the reports from him,
because he intended to divorce her.

Whether the one he addressed is divorced is subject to two reported positions of his. On the view that she is divorced, his followers differ over whether she is divorced only in the judicial ruling or inwardly as well,
following two approaches of theirs.

His words ﷺ, “Actions are by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended,” have been cited as proof that contracts by which one inwardly aims to reach something unlawful are invalid,

such as sale contracts by which the substance of usury and the like is intended, as is the position of Mālik, Aḥmad and others; for in such a contract it is usury that is intended, not sale, “and every person shall have only what he intended.”
The questions of intention connected with jurisprudence are very many, and what we have mentioned is sufficient.
It has already been mentioned that al-Shāfiʿī said of this hadith that it enters into seventy chapters of jurisprudence. Allah knows best.

Intention is the heart’s aim, and it is not obligatory to pronounce what is in the heart in any act of worship. Some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers derived from his teaching a view that pronouncing the intention is a condition of the prayer,
but the meticulous scholars among them judged this a mistake. The later jurists differed over pronouncing the intention in prayer and elsewhere: some considered it recommended and some disliked it.

Nothing specific is known to have been transmitted on these questions from the Salaf or from the imams, except regarding the Ḥajj alone. Mujāhid said: When he intends Ḥajj, he names what he is entering into; and he is reported to have said: He names it in the talbiyah. But this is not what we are discussing,
for the Prophet ﷺ used to mention his rite in his talbiyah, saying: “Here I am, for ʿUmrah and Ḥajj.” What we are discussing is whether he should say, when he wants to enter iḥrām:
O Allah, I intend Ḥajj, or ʿUmrah — as many jurists considered recommended — and Mujāhid’s words are not explicit on that.

Most of the Salaf, among them ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and al-Nakhaʿī, said: The intention when beginning the talbiyah is enough. It is authentically reported from Ibn ʿUmar that he heard a man say as he entered iḥrām: O Allah, I intend Ḥajj, or ʿUmrah. He said to him: Are you informing people?
Does Allah not know what is in your soul?
Mālik stated something similar explicitly: that it is not recommended for him to name what he has entered iḥrām for.
The author of Tahdhīb al-Mudawwanah, one of his followers, related this. Abū Dāwūd said: I said to Aḥmad: Do you say anything before the takbīr — meaning in the prayer?
He said: No. This may imply that he does not pronounce the intention. Allah knows best.
